title: Fenwick Tree (BIT)
tagline: Prefix sums with updates in O(log n) — using the lowbit trick on a flat array.

intuition.analogy: Think of measuring distance with a clever ruler whose marks cover 1, 2, 4, 8… units. Any length is the sum of a few such marks — so you reach any point in a handful of jumps rather than counting every unit.
paragraphs: A Fenwick tree (Binary Indexed Tree) supports two operations in O(log n): update a single position and query a prefix sum. Plain prefix arrays give O(1) queries but O(n) updates; a Fenwick balances both.

Each index i is responsible for a range of size lowbit(i) = i & (−i) — the value of its lowest set bit. Index 12 (1100₂) covers 4 elements; index 8 (1000₂) covers 8. This partition lets any prefix be assembled from O(log n) responsible nodes.

Update walks UP by adding lowbit (i += i & −i), touching every node whose range includes i. Query walks DOWN by subtracting lowbit (i −= i & −i), summing each responsible block. The bit magic makes both paths short.
intuition.keyIdea: Node i covers lowbit(i) elements; query and update each touch only O(log n) nodes via the lowbit jump.

steps.title: 1-indexed array tree[]
steps.detail: tree[i] stores the sum of the lowbit(i) elements ending at index i.

steps.title: update(i, delta)
steps.detail: Add delta at i, then move i += i & (−i) until past n — updating every node responsible for i.

steps.title: query(i)
steps.detail: Sum tree[i], then move i −= i & (−i) until 0 — accumulating the responsible blocks that tile [1, i].

codes.source:
class Fenwick:
    def __init__(self, n):
        self.n = n
        self.tree = [0] * (n + 1)
    def update(self, i, delta):          # 1-indexed point update
        while i <= self.n:
            self.tree[i] += delta
            i += i & (-i)
    def query(self, i):                  # prefix sum over [1..i]
        s = 0
        while i > 0:
            s += self.tree[i]
            i -= i & (-i)
        return s

complexity.timeReason: Each step flips off or adds the lowest set bit, so at most log n steps.
complexity.spaceReason: A single array of size n+1.

pitfalls: Fenwick trees are 1-indexed — index 0 is unused and would loop forever.
lowbit relies on two's complement; i & (−i) isolates the lowest set bit.
Range updates need either two BITs or a difference-array variant.

dryRun.clickMoment: Index 6 splits into block [5,6] (tree[6]) plus block [1,4] (tree[4]) — exactly two nodes cover six elements. The binary representation of 6 dictates which blocks to add.

problems.statement: Support point updates and range-sum queries.

approach: A Fenwick tree (BIT) supports point updates and prefix sums in O(log n).
update(i, delta) walks indices upward by i += i&-i; query(i) walks down by i -= i&-i. A range sum is query(r) - query(l-1).

problems.title: Count of Smaller Numbers After Self
problems.statement: Count smaller elements to the right.
problems.hint: Coordinate-compress values; BIT over value frequencies, processed right to left.

approach: Count, for each element, how many later elements are smaller. Process right-to-left, querying a BIT indexed by value rank.
Coordinate-compress the values to ranks. query(rank-1) gives how many already-seen (to the right) values are smaller, then add the current rank.

problems.statement: Count pairs with a[i] > 2·a[j], i < j.
problems.hint: BIT over compressed values with the 2x condition.

approach: Reverse pairs (i<j with a[i] > 2·a[j]) can be counted with a BIT over compressed values, scanning left-to-right.
For each a[j], first count earlier values greater than 2·a[j] (query the suffix of ranks), then insert a[j]'s rank.

problems.title: Number of Longest Increasing Subsequence (BIT)
problems.statement: LIS length and count via a BIT keyed on value.
problems.hint: BIT storing (best length, count) prefix maxima.

approach: Track LIS length and the number of LIS simultaneously with a BIT keyed by value rank, where each node stores the best (length, count) over a prefix.
For each value, query smaller ranks for the best length and its total count; the new state is (best+1, count or 1). Merge into the BIT, combining equal lengths by adding counts.
